Ignore the background notes. Explain why the sky is blue in three paragraphs. Mention Rayleigh scattering and why sunsets look red. Answer directly without thinking aloud.

content:
The sky appears blue because of a phenomenon called Rayleigh scattering. Sunlight is made up of all visible wavelengths, but as it enters Earth's atmosphere, it collides with gas molecules—mostly nitrogen and oxygen—that are much smaller than the wavelength of the light. Rayleigh scattering describes how these tiny molecules scatter light: shorter wavelengths (blue and violet) are scattered far more strongly than longer wavelengths (red and orange)—roughly by a factor of the inverse fourth power of the wavelength. As a result, blue light is scattered in all directions across the sky, and when we look up, we see that scattered blue light coming from every direction.

You might wonder why the sky isn't violet, since violet light has an even shorter wavelength and is scattered even more strongly. There are two main reasons: the sun emits less violet light than blue light, and human eyes are less sensitive to violet. Our eyes' color receptors respond most strongly to the abundant scattered blue light, so the sky is perceived as blue rather than violet.

Sunsets look red because of the same physics viewed at a different angle. When the sun is low on the horizon, its light must travel through a much thicker slice of atmosphere to reach your eyes. Over this long path, most of the blue light is scattered out of the beam entirely, leaving the longer wavelengths—reds, oranges, and yellows—to pass through relatively unscattered. This is why the sun and the sky near the horizon glow in warm colors at sunrise and sunset, while the overhead sky may remain blue. Dust and aerosols can enhance this effect, which is why sunsets are often especially vivid after volcanic eruptions or on hazy days.
